elements.texte:
[cheerful] New lesson: first value, last value and N-tile.

Read the first or last value of a window, and split the rows into equal groups.
elements.apres: For its various teams, NutriBoost is redoing the detailed page of the 8 products currently in the catalog.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] For its various teams, NutriBoost is redoing the detailed page of the 8 products currently in the catalog.

Each page shows its price tier and the most expensive product in its category.

The name, price and category are in the products table.

Two window functions are enough to solve the problem: first value and N-tile.

elements.apres: First value of name returns the name of the window’s first row.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] First value of name returns the name of the window’s first row.

Partition by category forms one window per category.

Order by price descending puts the most expensive product first.

In the Wellness category, the three products are sorted from most to least expensive.

In the Wellness category, Prebiotic Fiber comes first after sorting by descending price.

First value so returns its name on every row of the category.

Unlike group by, no row disappears.

elements.apres: For the cheapest one, we try last value of name, the last row.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] For the cheapest one, we try last value of name, the last row.

We expect Magnesium, the cheapest in the Wellness category.

Surprise: each row gets its own name.

Only Magnesium gets the right value.

elements.apres: With order by, the window has a default frame.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] With order by, the window has a default frame.

This frame goes from the first row up to the current row.

For Omega 3, the frame therefore stops at Omega 3.

As in sliding windows, rows between extends the frame to the whole window.

This time, all three rows get Magnesium.

First value doesn’t have this problem: the first row is always in the frame.

elements.apres: Next, the price tier: N-tile of 3 splits the rows into 3 groups.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Next, the price tier: N-tile of 3 splits the rows into 3 groups.

The 8 products are sorted from most to least expensive.

The groups are as equal as possible; if rows are left over, the first groups get one more row.

Since 8 isn’t divisible by 3, the first groups get one more row.

Result: 3 products in tier 1, 3 in tier 2 and 2 in tier 3.

[cheerful] We want to get two new pieces of information for each product: its price tier and the most expensive product in its category.

N-tile of 3 ranks all the products by price and splits them into 3 tiers.

First value of name separates the products by category, sorts them from most to least expensive, then gets the first name.

The complete query combines the two blocks, and also shows the category.

This query gives each product its tier and shows the most expensive product in its category.

Marine Collagen, in tier 1, comes first in the Beauty category.

The 8 product pages are ready to be published.
